newsitem.title: FRANCE: Club Med shares slump on profit outlook.
newsitem.headline: Club Med shares slump on profit outlook.

text.p: Shares in the French resort company Club Mediterranee plummeted on Wednesday after the group said weak vacation spending would hurt its peak season results.

After an early trading suspension triggered by a drove of selling orders, the share slumped nearly 20 percent before steadying slightly above its lows at 327 francs ($63.4), down 18 percent, at 1300 GMT.

The group announced on Tuesday evening that it expected flat pre-tax, pre-exceptional profit for the second half of its fiscal year, which runs to October 31. Last year's second half pre-tax, pre-exceptional profit was 25 million francs.

"The overall business climate in continental Europe has exacerbated the tendency of clients to seek out less expensive packages, particularly in the latter part of the summer," it said in a brief statement.

Brokerage houses slashed their earnings forecasts for the group and recommendations on the stock. French broker Cheuvreux de Virieu knocked the share off its list of recommended issues and advised clients to sell, portfolio managers said.
It cut its earnings-per-share (EPS) forecast for 1995/96 to 16 francs from 18.60 and for 1996/97 to 20 francs from 26.50.
SGE Delahaye switched its rating on Club Med's stock to 'underperform' from 'outperform' and cut its EPS forecast to 13.70 francs from 16.90 for 1995/96 and to 16.90 francs from 25.20 for 1996/97.
Dupont Denant and Transbourse lowered their ratings on the stock.
Paribas Capital Markets switched to 'sell' from 'neutral' and slashed its earnings estimates by 16 percent.
"Their major market is in a spending recession," said Paribas analyst Nigel Reed. He said French consumers, unnerved by record unemployment rates, were spending less on vacations.
The result is that Club Med's new lower priced Club Aquarius resorts are faring better than the more expensive Club Med "vacation villages", eroding the group's profit margins.

Analysts said the market's response was brutal because the company had not warned investors earlier about the trend. Last month chairman Serge Trigano said the company's profit target of 400 million francs for 1996/97 was achievable.
"The market feels deceived by statements that were too optimistic," one analyst said. "It's not just the figures that are poor, but their communication with investors."
A company official on Wednesday said the September forecast had assumed favourable economic conditions.
"Apparently the economic climate isn't what we were expecting," director Antoine Cachin told Reuters. But he declined to give a forecast for the current fiscal year or 1996/97.
The group is counting on an expansion in Asia, where consumers are beginning to feel more affluent, particularly in southeast Asia, to ensure long-term profit growth.
It plans to establish around 20 resorts in Asia by the year 2000 and increase the number of visitors to two million. It now has 102 "vacation villages" drawing 1.3 million visitors a year.

The group, which pioneered the all-inclusive holiday in which vacationers pay a set price for food, lodging and entertainment, has been struggling to recover from a severe slump in its business in the early 1990s.

Although its net attributable profit in 1994/95 of 169 million francs was a sharp improvement over the prior year's 94 million profit, it was dented by the impact on Club Med of the French nuclear testing last year in the Pacific. ($ = 5.157 French Francs)
